utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Esteemed honourable Judge Robinson, honourable Judge Harhoff, honourable Judge Mindua, also I wish to say good afternoon to my learned friends, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Edgerton, Mr. Docherty, and Mr. Sachdeva. Today we are going to put an end to our professional clash that we conducted to the best of our ability, and I must say that it was an honour to face such a wonderful team of Prosecutors. A few words about the proceedings themselves. It was a privilege to participate in perhaps the most expedient - so far - trial before this Tribunal, which I believe led to the fruition of the first principle envisaged by the Statute, namely, an expedient trial. It is not a meaningless principle and I can only wish that other trials had proceeded equally speedily without the accused waiting for years for the trial to begin. I also believe that the principle of a fair trial has been observed as well and the Defence has succeeded in raising all the issues that you will ultimately deliberate upon and conclude on. Maybe I could have done with a little more time to prepare for the argument today and maybe a little more time to produce the final brief, but anyway. Today at the beginning of my closing argument I want you to bear in mind that I have full understanding and sympathy for the witnesses like any normal human being. But today concerning the issues before you and the crimes, as they are called in the indictment, I have to speak professionally, with dignity, and I just have to ask you not to put me in a situation where I would have to answer questions like, Am I disputing that somebody lost their life. After many years of professional career, I had to do with serious crimes as well, but this is the first time I'm defending a person charged with thousands of murders. It is alleged here that my client is responsible, for instance, for 12 snipings and 19 incidents of shelling, which puts me in a difficult situation. Just before the start of this trial I have to say the Defence faced a rather big problem, namely, the stipulated facts. Perhaps this is not the right time to deal with these issues, but I will never cease to be sorry that we did not manage to introduce into evidence certain pieces of video footage that would show us a better picture and demonstrate that at the moment the conflict was starting it was something a bit different, something other than the -- than the civilian area that was depicted here. This area would have been shown to have been armed beforehand. It is only recently that books had begun to be written about this and evidence has started to emerge, but this is not the point I should be making now. My colleague warns me to slow down for interpretation. It is quite certain that we as the Defence team could have done a little better to demonstrate what had happened in that area in those first days of the conflict, but I believe that the Chamber was perfectly right in concluding that the background events are perhaps of marginal importance. The historic expert for the Prosecution finished his historical background with the 7th February 1994, and he did well because my primary interest as Defence counsel on behalf of my client is in the history that began on the 7th of February, 1994, after the decision was made to withdraw heavy weaponry 20 kilometres away from the centre of Sarajevo to a place called Marin Dvor. That is the history I will be dealing with. And since there are no major large-calibre political decisions in that particular segment of history, I will mainly be dealing with facts. It is not easy, Your Honours, to find oneself in a situation where you have a valid judgement against an accused who is sentenced to life, despite everything that I had mentioned earlier about the number of incidents involved, and to face a qualification that was formulated a little before the beginning of the trial; namely, that it was an inherited guilt. Inherited guilt, as far as I know, does not exist. That concept is foreign to criminal law, and I believe that this highest court of law, an international court of the United Nations, and this Chamber will bear that in mind. You know perfectly well that there is no judgement that cannot be varied in the light of new circumstances, and you know that even these rules of evidence and procedure stipulate clearly that an appeals judgement even can be varied if a new trial produces new facts that lead to new conclusions. That has already happened. It has happened in my career, in the country where I used to live, and in this country as well. There have been acquittals after retrial, but even if I had been the judge, even if I had already written my judgement, if I came across or somebody produced to me new evidence, even I, who does not change his opinion lightly, would find it incumbent upon me to rethink what I have already decided. It is my duty here in my position to bring new light to the matters covered by this earlier judgement, because if we proceed from the fact that a certain number of facts have been established already in a prior trial and these facts, regardless of the time and circumstances involved, can just be copied, transferred, on to another person, that would not be appropriate, it would not be consistent with the spirit of establishing criminal responsibility. I don't want you to think that I will only philosophise here, and I'm going to try to be direct. You know that this indictment focuses on a long-standing campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population of Sarajevo with the ultimate aim allegedly of spreading terror amongst the civilian population. These attacks, it is said in the indictment, resulted in many incidents of death and wounding. In this closing argument I have to emphasise that the main corpus of this criminal act alleged in the indictment, namely, that it was a civilian area and that it was an attack on civilians as such, in order for someone to be found responsible for this it must be established beyond any doubt that it was, indeed, a civilian area and that it was, indeed, a civilian population and that this man sitting today before you in the dock had no other intention than to use his powerful army against that civilian population. I will be dealing today with the facts that should demonstrate to the Trial Chamber whether for the entire duration of this conflict under both indictments, but particularly this one, it was indeed a civilian area. I had suggested a witness Ajdadzic at one point who described in his book the preparations for what was going to happen, the trenches that had been dug back in 1992. Unfortunately, I was unable to bring him and other witnesses, officers from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that could testify to that. The Prosecution brought two officers, one low-ranking and another one who led the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And you heard logically, primarily from civilians, victims, and exclusively the civilian police. I am going to show you a decision that shows that each of these policemen was a member of the BH Army. This is something that you should take into account in your deliberations. It was depicted by the Prosecution as an area that was practically free of any army, replete with civilian population that was heinously and mercilessly attacked, resulting in many deaths. I don't know whether I can find the one I'm looking for, but many documents are yet to emerge. I have to remember late Judge May, but Judge Robinson said at one point, "Those who survive shall see, those who live shall see." Similarly, I believe that the facts, the truth about everything that happened in this wretched country - and I'm not trying to glorify anything here - was due to a conflict that was needed by a handful of people. They started it all, each one of them got their own state, and some are about to get their own state but at the cost of many, many lives. Just a few days ago a document emerged, a very important document that you, Your Honours - and I'm very grateful to you for that - accepted, admitted into evidence. It has to do with everything that I will be dealing with today. It is a document whose authorship has not been established yet, but it is an official document nevertheless. It says, among other things ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague is reminding me, although I had no intention of mentioning -- am I allowed to use this document, Your Honours? I didn't think that it was necessary to go into closed session because the document that you accepted into evidence yesterday, that we tendered. It's a document that still has no DD005188. It still hasn't received a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what Defence alludes to, that's an excerpt from a diary which was given to the Prosecution under protection of Rule 70. I think it might be more cautious to go into private session if the Defence wants to raise that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thus we heard excerpts from a document that speaks of terrorism, not terror; these are two different things: Terrorism and terror. And I will show you through some very convincing evidence that there were acts of terrorism there as well. Some of these matters have been discussed at this trial, and a long time ago I showed a document to one of the witnesses, I'm not sure whether it is in evidence or not, concerning an explosion on the terrace of General Halilovic, whereby his brother and his wife were killed. It was said to be a shell from the VRS, but Halilovic himself is emphatic that it was a remote-controlled explosion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the difference between terrorism and terror?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terrorism is an individual act related to a specific situation, if you are requiring me to think freely about it. But terror is something that became a charge for the first time before this Tribunal. It was not envisaged before by international law. It is here at the ICTY that terror became one of the charges. It was not even in the first version of the Statute, but it will now certainly become part of legal history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't it in the Geneva Conventions and the Protocols -- Additional Protocol I? It's not a new crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would require a debate. I'm proceeding from the fact that -- from the assumption that it has already been verified by international law, and I would not like to go into this today. It is a matter for an entirely different, separate discussion, no matter how interesting the issue is in itself. Although I do want to move to the problem at hand, namely, the indictment in this case which deals with issues of terror. In order to do that, I have to refer to the allegation made by the Prosecution in the final brief, where on page 129, paragraph 469 it is said that by signing the anti-sniping agreement and by participating in negotiations on heavy weapons, the accused had effective control of the SRK, as obvious from the fact that casualties decreased for a while. It is even said in the brief that precisely the fact that Dragomir Milosevic signed the anti-sniping agreement proves that he had control over the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Not for a single moment will the Defence deny nor can the accused deny that he was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Having taken up that position, however, and having signed the anti-sniping agreement two days later, an agreement which would not have been signed, or rather, which was not able to be signed for a long time before that and there was pressure for it to be signed, and now this is used -- being used as an additional element to show premeditation on his part. They came to see him as the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to sign this; after that, the incidents decreased in number - and we'll see what sort of incidents they were. And now this is being used as evidence indicating the characteristics of his premeditation, his mens rea, whereas it's precisely the other way around in reality. The good will of one side, for example, yesterday it was mentioned that Karadzic said, Very well, we won't touch you, we won't touch the tunnel, and then it was again interpreted as a sign of malevolence on the side of Republika Srpska. In spite of the anti-sniping agreement, incidents continued. The OTP puts forward the example of a French soldier who was killed as evidence that all this continued. I now have to show you, for example, what an eminent witness before this Court, Harland said on page 399 to page 400, line 7. He said: "The representatives of the United Nations observed that the fighters of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were shooting at people on their own territory," and mark this, "in order to create panic. And for this reason the international factors protested with the Bosnian authorities." If you bear in mind the allegation that the SRK did everything it did in order to cause panic and everything else that was mentioned here, well, here you have indisputable evidence from the representatives of the United Nations who say that the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina themselves shot at themselves and their own people in order to give rise to panic. And finally, on page 395 from 18 to 24, this same witness said that soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were doing more shooting, you'll find that there, and I think he even added that they had so-called snipers, concealed marksmen. In the OTP brief, it says that this was a French soldier and that this was a breach of the anti-sniping agreement, but I will read out to you a letter from none other than Alija Izetbegovic, that's document D66, he was writing to one of his own commanders, saying that he had just come back from a meeting with the French ambassador and that he had been unpleasantly surprised to hear that there was evidence that out of 24 murders of their soldiers or 24 killings of UN soldiers -- or UN personnel, not counting those on Mount Igman, more than a certain percentage were done by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out again what Alija Izetbegovic wrote, that the French ambassador had told him that more than half of the 24 murders had been done by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document is D66, it was admitted into evidence a long time ago, and in the indictment it is further alleged that soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps - and this is very important for what Your Honours have to decide when considering sniping - sniping on trams -- well, there is indisputable evidence that it was done by soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska, that's what was said here, but in D67, on page 17, this is a report written by a policeman of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 28th of October. It was compiled on the 26th of October, 1994, concerning an event which occurred on the 25th, and all this is very important. And he says that on the 26th of October, 1994, he was sent out to observe the work of the UNPROFOR commission which had the task of establishing, by an on-site investigation of the tram, the direction from which shots were fired on the tram. And then he goes on to explain this, and then he says, On that side of the tram one could clearly see damage to the body of the car by bullets from infantry weapons. The holes that are a consequence of bullet hits, the UNPROFOR representative pushed some metal rods into these bullet-holes and said something to the people around him in French. The policeman had with him his own interpreter and he said the others in the team did nothing and said nothing. When I put a question, the interpreter said to me that the officer said that the shots had come from the Muslim side from a neighbouring white building which was in Sibenska Street, and the Bel Ami bar was in that building. The interpreter even said that the officer could even establish from which window the shots were fired. And you have a large number of incidents here of shooting at moving trams. If I have time, I will have to address this. There are even examples provided of crimes of intent to kill when a fragmentation bullet explodes and kills three to four people, you have several such incidents on this schedule concerning snipers who are supposed to target someone directly if they want to kill them. Your Honours, fortunately I have succeeded in obtaining irrefutable documents, I'm not making anything up. Let me tell you, I perhaps will not mention a single Defence witness, there are over 50 of them. I will refer exclusively to the testimony of Prosecution witnesses and the documents I have before me. Times have changed and we were able to go to the archive of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this may have been a slip on their part but this remained available, and I was able to see that soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired on their own people. And you know very well that everything that was shown, all the victims shown in the Sarajevo area were represented as victims of sniping by fighters of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Look at D48, a document signed by a colonel, the first and last name don't matter. He says: Yesterday on the 14th of October, 1994, one of our soldiers, soldier, well that's a question, but let's say he was a soldier, try to go over to the other side in the Grbavica area. Our soldiers opened fire and probably wounded him. Every attempt to cross over to the opposite side was punished by death. There is not a single shred of evidence nor will you ever be able to find any that any defector was shot by the Serb side while trying to cross over to the other side. There was a bridge that was open, the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge, which is long gone. And anybody who wanted to could cross over it. And anyone who did not do so there was shot at, just as this man was shot at, and that's not the only document. I have to show you D216, where a soldier boasts that from a tall building called Palma on the other side of the Miljacka River which was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - and I'm not making anything up I'm just giving you examples from documents - he observed someone trying to across over to the other side to defect and fire was opened and the rest is in the document. On the 3rd of November they fired on the escort of Mr. Silajdzic and that's 147, and this was represented as something done by the Serbs, but more importantly in document 205 it says that shots were fired at an elderly woman who tried to cross over to the other side and she was killed, according to his report, and brought back to the same side. That's D205. That's precisely what it says verbatim, shots were fired from Loris, a high-rise building on the other side of the Miljacka, it was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a document which is self-explanatory. And finally I have document 149 signed personally by Vahid Karavelic, who according to this document said, In the evening hours fire from infantry weapons was used to prevent a person defecting on Grbavica. And there's more of all this, but I don't think I need to explain what this means. This is irrefutable evidence showing who was shooting directly at civilians. I have some dozen documents showing that snipers have to have night sights and they must be active day and night, round the clock. For all this to make sense, Your Honours, and I'm going back to something I mentioned earlier, I don't want to abuse anybody's feelings here, but I'm forced to show three brief clips which all together -- all three together are no longer than three minutes in total. I wish to show them now. These tactics of committing crimes against one's own people and then portraying these crimes as having been committed by the other nation I think a journalist, a witness, Mr. Bell, said that nobody was innocent here, but on the Sarajevo front it was always only the Serbian side that was blamed. However difficult it is to watch this, such things were shown to the entire world as crimes committed by one side. In this television war, as Mohatarem termed it, it is well-known who the winner was and is, but things have to be put in their place and I think the only place to do so is the court. Regardless of whether something happened 12 years ago and a political or military judgement was passed after as little as 24 hours, let's now see before Your Honours based on irrefutable evidence what happened actually on the 28th of August, 1995. Is this not the same thing that happened in these individual incidents where a man was killed by an ordinary rifle while trying to defect to the other side? These three brief clips which I have to deal with, Your Honours, I have to say that I was in two minds as to whether I should show you only these three, the shelling of Markale in 1995, the hit on the television on the 28th of June, 1995, and what was established there -- has it been established beyond any reasonable doubt? No. I think it's quite the other way around. In one case it's quite certain that it has been established beyond any reasonable doubt that it was actually done by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So let's view these three clips briefly, these three clips which show the method, the tactics employed -- I'll come back to this if I have time to analyse it, to the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Waespi on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, can we have the exhibit numbers, please, of these three clips?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 620 -- P620, D91, and P623. I'm sorry, before we see this it was shown to the whole world, and based on this the whole world quite justifiably responded as it did. No one can view this with equanimity but one has to face the truth, Your Honours. And after all the evidence has been presented judge what happened. I will comment on one clip right away and the other two when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, while we are waiting for this video I would like to go back to what you've just said a moment ago concerning certain witnesses, apparently from the BHA, such Ajdadzic who would have said that even back in 1992 trenches were being dug. Could you tell me why these witnesses were unable to come or why you couldn't bring them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm glad, Your Honour, that you ask me that question. Of course that was one of our main ideas when we were preparing for this trial. Only two witnesses have been brought here which belonged to the top, the commanding top of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but to be quite truthful I was hoping these would be court witnesses, just as Hansen was. I may be wrong. He was, or rather, the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, is one of these; the commander of the 12th Division Prevljak and Ajdadzic who in the final stage of the war replaced Karavelic and then at the time of the NATO air strikes and a little before that became the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These were witnesses we were unable to establish contact with. These are the so-called hostile witnesses. It would have been futile to try. We did try a little, but what happened with Delic happened. He was here in the Detention Unit. I could have put just a few questions to him about the documents he signed. In these books where they now speak of their sly strategy, that has to do with the hills, that cunning strategy of theirs, and the conviction prevalent to this very day that the Serbs were up there on the hills overlooking Sarajevo and simply firing, but I think I have acquired or obtained documents which show the real truth of this. It would have been better had we been able to introduce these exhibits through these witnesses, but this was beyond our power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To move on to the key issue here as Defence counsel, I feel that unless this chief characteristic of the crime alleged against the accused is dealt with, that is, that this was a civilian area, that these were civilians as such and that they were fired at as civilians, well, let's see whether this actually was a civilian area and whether it can be described as such. All the time the number of 250.000 civilians was repeatedly mentioned. I thought that the OTP would be able to demonstrate on what basis it was estimated there were 250.000 civilians -- 250.000 civilians there. My learned friend Mr. Whiting in his closing argument said there was 78.000 soldiers there. However many civilians there were there, 250.000, there were 40.000 Serbs among them. And if I have time I'll come back to deal with this, these 40.000 Serbs down there were also held hostage by Serbs, they were hostages. And -- well, it's a moot point who was a hostage was down there. The side that was up there on the hills ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is right, who was whose hostage. I'll go on to deal with that later, but I wanted to point out something else now. Was it of any significance to those people who were up there on the hills that they had friends, relatives, maybe a brother or a sister down there? Could it have been easy for them to shoot, to fire from those hills unless they were forced to? I am speaking to the period of the indictment against General Milosevic. But let's first deal with those hills and Count 7 of the indictment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I just had the indictment handy, but I'm getting on, it seems. I apologise, Your Honours. I don't want to be imprecise. We often refer to Count 7 of the indictment where it says first that on the 7th of April, 1992, these separation lines were established. I think that in the course of these proceedings in paragraph 7 these lines were established in 1992, but what matters is here. In the indictment it says that after that the city was subjected to blockade and relentless bombardment and sniper attacks. Much of the bombardment and sniping was from positions in the hills around and overlooking Sarajevo from which the attackers had a clear, detailed, and commanding view of the city and its civilian population." It was with this conviction that all the witnesses you examined here arrived, including General Rupert Smith, Mohatarem, Butt, Demurenko even, one of the Defence witnesses, and they all spoke in this vein initially. When I asked witness Butt where his position had been he said on Mali Hum and in the further examination he confirmed quite clearly who was at Zuc and Hum, that big Hum. It was well-known here that it was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that held those two hills. When I asked Knustad, he was at Colina Kapa. Colina Kapa is one of the hills of Trebevic which is predominant, it overlooks everything, not far from the positions of Republika Srpska where the trenches were, and there is no doubt that the hill called Debelo Brdo was also taken by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to mention Mojmilo. All this was established through the testimony of international witnesses. But let me go back to the documents and the witnesses. These only two witnesses, soldiers belonging to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have a document here, D110, introduced through Witness Hadzic in the form of an order, I have this document before me now, the Chief of Staff, Colonel Rizvo Pleh ordered that all vital facilities, Grdonj, Borije, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Adzici, Stupsko Brdo, Vis, Zuc must have wire communications with both sides. It's a document that irrefutably shows that all the hills were held by the BH army. What's arguable perhaps is Grdonj, but even this Grdonj hill is a dominant feature, and even Spicasta Stijena which became notorious as far as the accused is concerned was under the control of the BH army. One of the witnesses clenched his fist here and showed you that a person who would reach the top would practically commit suicide. From that ridge it was impossible to fire. In any case, after looking at this document one could say that the VRS had perhaps higher and more dominant view at one point in Trebevic and at one point in Zlatiste and had a view of Sarajevo, one part held by the Bosnian side and Grbavica, Nedzarici, and Dobrinja held by the Serbian side. This order of the 20th March 1995 shows that howitzers were placed there on Hum, so many mortars, Mojmilo Brdo, Bresce Brdo, Majevica, let me not enumerate them all. There are more documents. This one is 418, another one is 195, all speaking of the disposition of heavy weapons on Mojmilo hill. At one point it says Mojmilo hill, direction of fire Zlatiste; another access of fire, Gavrica Hill. Not only did they therefore hold these hills. The BH army had its most powerful weapons on those hills, not the VRS, as it was concluded in the Galic case. This Tribunal -- the Prosecution, rather, is asking you to simply copy the facts established in Galic to this case. In paragraph 576 of the indictment it says that the Prosecution claims that the overpowering weaponry and ammunition and the territorial predominance held by the VRS should be the pivot of the criminal responsibility of the accused in that campaign against civilians in Sarajevo. So they're talking about geographic advantage and overpowering weapons. The Defence has shown that there was no geographic advantage and certainly no advantage in the level of armaments at the relevant period. We have shown that not only on the basis of a Defence witness's testimony but also international witnesses. I'm sorry that I could not bring journalist Van Lynden who testified in Galic but could not come here. It is on his evidence that important conclusions of the Trial Chamber in Galic are based. He said that because of the terrain, because Sarajevo is an elongated city running along Miljacka River and because the Bosnian Serbs held all elevations, it is possible to wipe out entire streets in Novo Sarajevo and in the centre of the town. He was the crown witness for the Prosecution; however, he couldn't come here. In Rasim Delic's book it is written that he had spoken to him on the 15th of January, 1995, after the meeting at Dudakovic and Van Lynden expressed his readiness to continue to report from all critical areas suggesting to appoint a group of reporters who would assert the just struggle of the army. Van Lynden and his evidence served as the basis of all those conclusions in the Galic case. In paragraph 144, which was taken as a stipulated fact, says SRK forces used and took advantage of natural topographic features. The evidence, however, shows that it was the BH army that took advantage of these natural elevations. And all this is shown in another paragraph, 146 to be based on Van Lynden's testimony. Now, as for the level of armaments on both sides of the relevant time, the period of the indictment, as far as the VRS is concerned I can be very brief. This exclusion zone was established on the 7th February 1994, and that is part of the legacy of Dragomir Milosevic. Some say that he could have done more as the second-ranking man in the VRS, leader of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and we have document P802 which claims that as the final brief of the Prosecution puts it on page 132, paragraph 484, they say that this document P802 shows that the accused five days after the agreement on the exclusion zone suggested that the use of heavy weaponry be resumed. He did say something similar, but that was just a suggestion at the moment when he was not the commander and when he cannot be held responsible in the terms alleged in the indictment. It was a suggestion that I would say is perhaps understandable at the time. It was winter-time and certain things were simply impossible to remove during the winter. It was all under the control of the UNPROFOR and the UNPROFOR was later satisfied that all had been done. But there is another document, D303, regarding heavy weaponry. This document was done on the 1st of January, 1995. What is held against Dragomir Milosevic concerns the 10th of February, 1994. This document, however, is dated 1st January 1995. Why am I saying this? Immediately after the signing of the cease-fire agreement which was supposed to last until April that year, we have this document of Rasim Delic who says there as far as heavy weaponry and its exclusion are concerned - let me just focus on the most important points - this process should not be hurried and weapons should not be placed under UNPROFOR control. Rasim Delic writes this on the 1st of January, 1995, whereas heavy weaponry had to be removed back in -- back in 1994 by 7th February. As opposed to this we have this charge against Dragomir Milosevic because of his suggestion, whereas we have a clear document of the BH Army showing that they had no intention of removing their weapons. True, in May when it was already quite certain that the BH Army would launch an offensive, although the Prosecution in their final brief emphasised that at time, the summer of 1995, Sarajevo was brought to its knees under the pressure of Milosevic's forces. But we didn't hear a single witness who denied that the Bosnian army's offensive started on the 16th of June, 1995. As far as the heavy weaponry is concerned, it was taken back from the UNPROFOR by both sides once the offensive started, and this document, D12, shows precisely that, that both sides started violating the exclusion zone resulting in 1500 explosions in one day, on Tuesday, and 1200 explosions on Wednesday. As far as combat in this civilian area is concerned, only on one day on the 16th of May and another day, the 25th of May, when the VRS was bombarded by NATO, from Sarajevo, from BH-held Sarajevo, 1.000 80-millimetre and 120-millimetre and 60-millimetre shells were fired. If the allegation is that one Serbian shell killed 43 on the Bosnian side, then how many on the Serbian side were killed by a thousand shells? I'm not making this up. This transpires from the documents found in the archives of the BH army. Let us look, honourable Judges, at what happened with the weaponry of the BH army in this critical period. Let us take only General Rupert Smith on page 3359-16, 17 he said that the BH army was not always stronger in numbers, but they were getting new weapons. Rupert Smith assumed his position in the force that will launch air-strikes against the VRS. On page 3358-12-13 he says he was aware that Bosnian troops and supplies were moving through the tunnel all the time. An international UN representative says on page 329, Weapons reached Muslims thanks to the support of the Islamic community throughout the world. On page 416 it is said that the Bosnian side was getting a lot of weaponry all the time, but they never received heavy weapons or tanks, that's what he said here, but in the document that he wrote, and that's document P19, that's what he said on the 2nd of July, reporting to his superiors. "Since the Bosnian offensive started two weeks ago, the number of Bosnian heavy weapons used in the vicinity of UNPROFOR installations has increased. Some people in the UNPROFOR see in this a Bosnian intention to provoke an anti-artillery attack by the UNPROFOR that would thus be involved in the conflict against the Serbs." But the main point for us is this, that the number of heavy weapons in use was increased and that the concentration of heavy weapons is not larger in the vicinity of UNPROFOR installations but elsewhere. Thus, the entire area in Bosnian hands in Sarajevo was covered by heavy weapons. Harland states this not once, but repeats it on page 378 and 379. The witness confirmed that the tunnel was in use continuously throughout the indictment period, and the tunnel was used for the transport of weapons and ammunition. Another witness, Mr. Mohatarem who spoke about the media war and the TV war, the theatre, as he put it, he said on page 751, Serbs are now in a weaker position because the Bosnian army is now stronger in numbers, is receiving better weaponry. That was at the time of the offensive. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I hope this will be the last time. I'm going to make an effort not to intervene again. We have heard a lot of witnesses, Prosecution and Defence witnesses, but obviously - and you will correct me if I'm wrong - all those witnesses said that the BH had more personnel than the SRK. But on the other hand, maybe because of what was inherited from the JNA, the SRK had more weapons. You obviously spoke about one of the witnesses who said that towards the end certain countries, certain Muslim countries helped the Muslim side achieve a position of superiority. I'm not sure if it's on this basis that you say that the BH was better equipped and had more weapons than the SRK or is it maybe that -- is it maybe that following this agreement on the exclusion of heavy weapons and because of the winter season, General Milosevic's troops could not move their weapons in the particular terrain, and that is why they found themselves out-gunned. So what I'm asking you is you seem to be saying that contrary to what the witnesses say, practically the SRK was not as well equipped in terms of guns as some witnesses say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you have not read the footnotes in our brief where we mention a great number of evidence attesting to the fact that the BH army in the period of the indictment was much better armed than the VRS. I noted many documents to respond to the claims of the Prosecution. On the 7th of February it was already the last days of winter, the weapons were removed towards Nisici and Trnovo. Sporadically in places the army left something behind perhaps, but generally the UNPROFOR verified all this and concluded that the heavy weaponry was removed, and whatever weapons were left behind were put in storage under UNPROFOR control. I just showed you a BH army document that says that they had not done so in January 1995. When I say that the VRS was out-gunned, I mean, first of all, that the heavy weaponry was removed 20 kilometres away, whereas the BH army kept arming and re-arming throughout that period and that the embargo did not really apply to it. The exclusion zone that should have come into effect back in 1993 became ever more replete with weapons and the communication between the fighters in Sarajevo and in Central Bosnia was never interrupted. They used the tunnel, which many witnesses testified was used to resupply and replenish the BH army. You interrupted me at the perfect place, and I wish you interrupted me more often in this way because this has been very useful. Because right now if you have finished I have another document that provides irrefutable evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First of all it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honour, Judge Mindua, I may not have been sufficiently clear in the course of my arguments. I am quoting mostly from what others have said concerning arming. I have before me a document which, in the most convincing and well-argumented way, shows how the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina armed itself in the indictment period, that's D305, and it is a tape-recording from a session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in August 1995 at which there was a serious discussion between the supreme commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Prime Minister, Mr. Silajdzic. In the course of this discussion it was shown in an indisputable way how the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had armed itself before and during the indictment period and was still arming itself. And I will give you but a few examples. For example, in an argument with Silajdzic, Izetbegovic said, "In the past 15 days alone we have brought in 26 air-lifts of weapons." Who flew these weapons in? Do any of you know who flew them in? Do the people know who did it? These are anonymous people, completely anonymous people. 26 air-lifts. The man who came had been in Germany, the wounded one, he was away for two years. He knows what the army was like in 1992. He came back and he says the army's unrecognisable. This is a real army, it's now well-armed and well-trained. This is what Alija said and he repeated it more than once. And then he points out the following. 26 cargo planes arrived over the past few days, 10.000 rockets from multiple rocket-launchers, and then air bombs, and other weapons. And then Silajdzic said that his sister, the ambassador in Pakistan who had resigned, was taking care of the delivery of weapons by ships and planes. One ship had arrived recently and been intercepted by NATO, and then $2 billion for weapons are mentioned. And then, for example, Silajdzic says concerning weapons procured in Turkey and there was some problems about this, he says the people who are doing this, trust me, I know who these people are. I know these people, you don't. These are people who did not sleep for nights on end loading ships in far away countries. And then he compares that to those 26 air-lifts. So that was all taking place at the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have this exhibit, it's D305. The supreme commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the prime minister are vying with each other concerning the amounts of weapons brought in by air or by ship, and then Rasim Delic gets mixed up in all this and talks about the time when he took over the army in 1993 when it was a paramilitary force and now he says the following: "I can tell you that as of June last year," and this is taking place in the summer of 1994, so he is referring, or rather, the Presidency meeting took place in the summer of 1995 and he says that the year before as of June, so that's 1994, "as of June last year we have been in a strategic position not just to defend ourselves, but to take the initiative." The chief of the General Staff Rasim Delic said this and he mentioned June which is more or less the time just before Dragomir Milosevic took over command. Not to mention P336, a document of the Army of Republika Srpska, we can have our reservations about what it says, but they say that there are about 270.000 soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who already have 120 tanks. But I will round off this topic and I will go on to speak about the geographical situation and the situation concerning weapons, or rather, I will recapitulate. In the time-frame concerning Galic, the BH army had gained supremacy in territory and weapons, and as regards the army Dragomir Milosevic inherited another thing and that was the sanctions. In addition to the international embargo which never applied to the Muslim side, there was now an embargo from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Serbian state. As of that point in time, not a single weapon arrived. There is no evidence to show that any did arrive. The number of men did not increase by a single soldier. I won't mention who submitted this report, but it says that - and this is in evidence - it concerns a report where it says that the SRK at the time of the offensive had 13 to 15.000 soldiers and the soldiers were for the main part reservists recruited locally in Sarajevo. They lived there with their families as was the custom in the former Yugoslav military system. So 13 to 15.000, that's an excellent estimate. At the time all this began, there were 18.000 and at the time of the offensive there were 15.000. And this was reported by an eminent officer in a high-ranking position. What happened to these people? They were killed in the fighting which had gone on for years. What did they die of? What were they killed by? Was it because they were spreading terror? If they were the ones spreading terror, how could so many of them have got killed? The terror that my learned friend spoke about, the primordial fear which the primal fear, this fear was there for everyone, it was felt by everyone, civilians and soldiers alike. If someone had a strategy of terrorising and killing civilians, it would not have been possible for several thousand of their soldiers to be killed. There is a church that has been built on Mount Romanija overlooking Sarajevo and so far the names of 3.000 victims, Serb soldiers, have been inscribed on the walls, have been engraved in the stone. So all this shows that that area was a theatre of heavy fighting, of serious conflicts, and one cannot characterize this as a civilian area and speak of civilians as the sole targets at the time of the events in this indictment. I will speak about this even more precisely at the end of my closing arguments, but there is indisputable evidence in writing showing that in August 1994 there was a certain number of men, 18.000, and in the 1st Corps alone there was 67 to 68.000 men. If you consider that the units of the 3rd Corps amounted to 34.000, the 4th Corps amounting to 15.000, the 7th Corps 32.000, along with the police forces also participated - and I have evidence about the police forces - this amounts to 140 to 150.000 men. Judge Robinson, at one point you told me that I should not allow myself to make such estimates off the top of my head, but now I'm showing you documents which indicate this. So 130 to 140.000 men participated in the offensive in the summer of 1995, and this is the time when the OTP said Sarajevo was on its knees. I have a number of documents here. I cannot dwell on them too long, but let's take an example. Witness 140, W-140, on page 2117/17-25 and 2118/1, 2, 3, that's a policeman who was conducting those investigations and I'll come back to those later on, said that everyone in Sarajevo was armed, all the policemen in Sarajevo, that is, were armed, and he knew that the police force was part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Document D3 -- 133 contains something very important, although it's part of a book, but one can see that it's a decision issued by Alija Izetbegovic: "All units of the reserve forces of the Ministry of Interior Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are hereby resubordinated to the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to carry out combat operations against the aggressor." At the time of the offensive there were about 150.000 men who set out on the offensive. I think there is no doubt about that, and I must mention this although it may not be so important but I must mention it because it strengthened the desire to protect one's life and limb. It's -- it may not be important for the indictment, but it is for the Defence, and that's document -- Defence document 145 which is again a report of the security service saying that in this offensive, the summer offensive, one of these corps, I think the 7th Corps, will have a Mujahedin unit in its composition. And it is well-known that this Mujahedin unit does not take prisoners of war. If you know that someone like that is participating in an action against you, then of course your defence must be very persistent. I showed you this document a long time ago and it bears a certain weight in all this. And now it's very important to point out how this area of combat operations was broadened and what the significance of the tunnel was. The tunnel had a multiple significance: It was humanitarian but also used for military purposes. It practically annulled certain things. With the help of the tunnel and the geographic prevalence of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina it -- this led to broadening of the area of combat operations. David Harland said on 374/12, 375/2, the existence of the tunnel made it possible for General Delic to have complete control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Sarajevo in the part which was under the control of that army, and that part of Sarajevo had full communication with the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Central Bosnia. As of that point there is constant cooperation between the units in Central Bosnia and the units active in the area of responsibility within Sarajevo. And after that one can no longer speak of an area within Sarajevo because according to the testimony of Witness Hadzic the troops mainly rested in Sarajevo and went through the tunnel into the fighting going on at Nisici and Trnovo. He went on to say that the Muslims indeed used the tunnel for military purposes to conduct attacks against the Serbs in other areas, and then they would come back to the town. And that was one of the reasons why the tunnel had been dug. That's what Witness Harland said on page 378/1-379/9. And Muhammed Mohatarem W-44 confirmed that the tunnel was used for the entry and exit of soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the actions on Mount Igman and therefore the tunnel could be a military target. This is on page 743/22-744/3. Rupert Smith confirmed that the troops coming in and going out of the tunnel were military target 3351/13-17 and he went on to add that he knew that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used the tunnel, but he was not informed as to the direction they were leaving in, 3371/12-14. Then you have these documents, D52 and D -- D152 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And D304 which show beyond doubt how the units moved through that tunnel, according to what roster or schedule in order to prepare properly to go out and carry out combat tasks outside the Sarajevo theatre, as is mentioned here, and that's how we can establish based on these documents something very significant with the help of their superiority in weapons, their geographic position which was superior, and their superiority in manpower which they had always had and the possibility of having normal communications through the tunnel, at least when military operations were concerned, all this led to a change in the tactics of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's set out with crystal clarity in document P492, that's a Prosecution document, and I will draw your attention to a part which is indisputable and follows from what the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Vahid Karavelic stated here. He said the following: "Therefore, in 1994 we changed our tactics and we tried to take a large part of our forces outside the city to make it possible to have a battle in the areas outside Sarajevo, manoeuvre, combat operation." And he went on to add: "In early 1994 we went into a counter-attack and many of our forces were deployed outside the city because we had concluded the city could not be maintained. In the course of 1994 we restored a lot of the territory we had lost during the VRS offensive. And most importantly, we tried to encircle part of the VRS forces surrounding Sarajevo." So who was surrounded now in Dragomir Milosevic's time? Who was under siege? In the presence of a tunnel which had broadened the areas of combat operations on the one hand and on the other hand in the presence of all these other factors in which the BH Army was superior, such as arms, geographic advantages and the advantage in personnel. Karavelic also said on page 4142, 19-22: "In these tactics, the tunnel was used only for military purposes and to supply the city with weapons." He stated that before you here. In addition to what is contained in this document. What else could this have led to but for the people in Nisici, Trnovo, and Grbavica, and in other places to defend themselves, to try to save themselves because very few of them were left. Now, let's look at this from another vantage point. There is no doubt that civilians were mixed in with soldiers, for example, Witness Nicolai, W-98 confirmed and explained his previous statement in which he said that snipers were sometimes soldiers and sometimes civilians carrying weapons and that every man and boy in Sarajevo was armed and that the military authorities were able to control their soldiers but not the armed civilians. Your Honours, the statement of a foreign observer, officer Eimers is very significant, that's document 585. In addition to what he stated here directly, that is, that civilians were used to carry out military operations, he said, and I have to read this from his report: "when we once established where it was," he's referring to mortars, "we would either arrive too late or we would not have permission to go in." And this is very important, he said: "They never opened fire from the same location twice so that when we arrived it would already be too late." And there's a statement that remains here in relation to that worst event that the forces of Republika Srpska held mortar positions for a year in the same place and that they were able to read the target. And this is incomprehensible, that they would only have to pull the trigger and two years later they would still be able to hit the same target. Your Honours will have to evaluate such statements, I'll come back to this later, but let's hear what else Eimers has to say: "When they shot at the exit and entry points to the tunnel," he's referring to the Serbian side now, "when there was civilians and soldiers, you would never know who started shooting first. In that context discussion of civilian victims became ever more serious. The Bosnian army did nothing to protect civilians in the tunnel area and that's what protected their operations. The special feature of that tunnel was that it was used by both civilians and soldiers." He then goes on to speak about Hrasnica and says that nobody controlled the soldiers. There was civilian authorities there, but they all had to answer to the brigade commander, whereas the Prosecutor says that Hrasnica was a civilian area and one of the pieces of evidence is the statement of Witness Dukic, who said that it was a civilian area in 1992, but then he was arrested and until January 1995 he was in prison. But now this witness is allegedly able to confirm that Hrasnica was a civilian area. He goes on to say that artillery fire was not fired on mortar positions in response. Both sides had mortars which they handled well. Then he goes on to speak of victims and then he mentions the following. "The army of the Bosnian Serbs, firing from Ilidza, from anti-aircraft weapons would hit civilian vehicles on the road." But then he goes on to say: "The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did, indeed, use civilian vehicles for logistics, both for military and for civilian purposes on that road. And one could not know whether there were soldiers or civilians in the vehicle. There were trucks on which machine-guns or heavy anti-aircraft weapons were loaded." And then he finishes by saying that the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina broke off all contact with him in the winter of 1994/1995 because, he says, "In the course of the winter the Bosnian army received support and supplies from the Americans. We saw them reconnoitring all over Sarajevo to establish where they could succeed." That is a statement by Officer Eimers, a Prosecution witness who found time to come and testify here from a distant front line in Asia. This mixture of civilians and soldiers shows in the best possible way to what extent this was something which could in no way be referred to as a civilian area. This witness Dervisa Selmanovic was a member of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and she was told at work not to wear a uniform because she would be safer if she was wearing civilian clothes, that's page 603/9-12. And Your Honours know very well how this is regulated by international law. Eimers said something else here before you on page 480/9-21, he says that soldiers were ordinary citizens during the day and they would go to the military positions by night, to the east and west of Mount Igman. When crossing from their houses to the trenches they did not always wear military clothes, so it was difficult to establish whether, in the course of these movements, they were carrying out military activities. I don't want to spend a lot of time on what witnesses said here before that Prosecution map, 194. Witness Hadzic, who explains certain things, Witness Eimers, I think W-40, 40 and 42, Witness Veljovic, Mohatarem who spoke of a depth of 2 kilometres and who said that military targets were in a 2-kilometre zone from the area -- from the demarcation line. And in view of his great military experience he said that the Presidency building could be a military target. Then there's a Witness W-101 who said that brigade staffs were -- or brigade headquarters were in ordinary buildings, that's on page 1061. Or Witness W-42 who said that residential buildings in the urban area could equated with trenches, that's page 1862/12-18, 64/11. Or Witness W-46 who spoke of the entrance to the tunnel from the Butmir side which was in an ordinary house and at Dobrinja in the middle of residential buildings. Your Honours, that was the situation as it relates to the problem of or the issue of what sort of area this was. And if it is not proven beyond any doubt that it was a civilian area, then the Defence has nothing further to tell you about any other alternatives, it is not up to us to deal with that. I don't know how much you will deal with it if you conclude that this was a civilian area, but in any case it is my deep conviction based on irrefutable evidence it was not a civilian area. I hope I will have more time to say more about it later. Civilians, not only were not the sole target, they were not a target at all. I will illustrate this by specific examples. What happened was fighting and combat operations that went on throughout the indictment period. If you remember, when I spoke about these matters after the Prosecution case under Rule 98 bis, I mentioned this campaign, using examples to illustrate, not really dealing with combat operations, but just pointing to a minor problem that cannot be of decisive importance in deciding on the mens rea of the accused. I said on that occasion that there were certain periods which cannot be qualified as any sort of campaign. I spoke about the period from August 1994 until April or May 1995. There were combat operations then, but certainly not risk a campaign. Everything had gone downhill and everything would have ended well if other people had not had other plans and if there had been no offensive. I will have a couple of documents to show you on this issue as well. Because, Your Honours, some people may have had different plans at the beginning of the war, there were all sorts of people there who had different designs and objectives. I won't go into that because I'm not that interested in that as Defence counsel. What matters to me are the people in the trenches and what they did. You know very well and you have heard a lot of evidence that with the start of the conflict 100.000-plus people left, the greatest number of them Serbs, and all of them who had apartments and houses there stayed in Sarajevo and went into the trenches to fight. Those who originated from Sarajevo stayed in Sarajevo and spent the whole war there. No one else was there, only the natives, including General Dragomir Milosevic. In any case, all those people had been decimated and were clutching at straws to remain there. Now, about orders and who was able to issue them under those circumstances, you can, for instance, look at the report of Mr. Harland or his evidence here. It is typical. He said on page 385, lines 14 to 23, he said that after the truce in February the Muslim side violated the agreement on the cease-fire 318 times. He goes on to say on page 384, lines 22, Serbs sincerely wanted the situation to stabilise in Sarajevo and they stopped their operations, decreasing operations and combat on the separation lines all the way until February 1994. Whatever plans existed in some other time, whatever the reasons for maintaining what Ms. Edgerton named the status quo situation, in the minds of one side this belief really existed, not only because that territory was taken by occupiers and cleansed from the Muslim population, Serbs were cleansed from Sarajevo. Defence has documents showing what happened in the month of May and how many people were killed in Pofalici when they tried to escape from Sarajevo so that nothing really happened there except that by the same token some Muslims had to leave neighbourhoods where they were in the minority. That happened, although people had lived for years quite peacefully side by side and nobody really needed any of this. It is absolutely not true that those locals had any strategic plans, but even if those plans existed at this moment, whatever the situation, they had no longer any desire to continue with this. And negotiations were going on that were supposed to lead to a final solution. Some parties, however, found this inconvenient and the Defence will show the real culprit for the failure of the agreement to be extended in that month of April. We have VRS documents, including document 214, as I said, document 214 and other documents. For instance, the document from April 1995 which says that certain actions would be taken only if an offensive is launched. Document 141 speaks volumes about this. It says: "We have information that the enemy is preparing action against the corps and in order to thwart these plans I hereby order." Everything was in this same spirit such as we see from document 186 which mentions Bascarsija and Vrbanja neighbourhoods. It says that action can be taken only on the orders of the commander of the SRK, emphasising the assignments that have to be accomplished have to do with neutralising fire points, machine-gun nests, and other fire points that prevented people from movement in Grbavica, Kasindol, and other areas. I can even mention a document authored by Mladic on the 31st of March, 1995, that's a document of the Prosecution, P337, which also speaks about defending the territory. It's only one aspect of this matter, the plans of the Army of Republika Srpska to stabilise the situation, and an honest desire to do so, quite unlike the opposing side. As David Harland says on page 386, lines 1 to 12, not only were there 300 and so violations, BH violations of the cease-fire agreement, but in the following months up to June there were another 196 violations. And then he says the Muslims did not want the situation to stabilise, and that was frustrating to General Rose. Just look at this amount of violations at the stage when it was agreed for the cease-fire to continue. Look at document D3 of the 18th of September when the first fierce combat occurred. Izetbegovic says, according to Harland, that he wanted to provoke the Serbs into opening fire on the city, which they reluctantly did. And that provided Izetbegovic with a strong negotiating chip with the US about lifting the embargo. There is another document, P816, it's a conclusion. On the bright side General Rose blamed the attack on Muslims depriving them of the advantage on the international plane as far as positive reporting by the media is concerned. "If they repeat such provocations, I believe that they will at least be careful enough to camouflage them better."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have just about exhausted two hours. How much more time are you going to need? I'm not prepared to give you more than the Prosecutor used, which was an additional 34 minutes. Mr. Waespi, are you going to want another bite at the cherry?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I do have just a few minor comments on what the Defence has said so far, nothing major, but I would love to have some time to respond, yes, if I'm allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see it's provided for in the Rules. I don't understand why, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, you drafted the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I didn't draft that, I can tell you, because we don't have it in our system. You make your closing address and that's it. How does it become appropriate to speak of a rebuttal? That's when you're leading evidence, taking evidence. It's not relevant in closing argument, but if you wish then I'll give you a very short time, seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll think about it. Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I not reckon with a small extension?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you can -- yes, I'm willing to give you another 34 minutes, which is as much as the Prosecutor had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, how much longer would you need? You would then have had two hours and 34 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until 6.00. If I could get until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ten minutes to 6.00, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, Your Honours, I would have to try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can hardly quote all these orders properly, but at least I will try to point out let's say the 16th of November. The BH army fired four mortar projectiles from the area encircled by Presidency buildings, the residences of the Kosevo Hospital. The projectiles exploded in Rajlovac area and Slatino Brdo. On the next day the transformer station was targeted, nine projectiles hit a civilian area controlled by the VRS. Those are the combat operations, the acts that the Prosecution qualifies as civilian areas, areas from which the VRS should not have responded. Take document 157 which says: "The BH army has grown into a powerful military force." It's dated 19th September, 1994, just as General Milosevic took over his position. The document was signed by Rasim Delic. There are many other documents of -- about this offensive action signed by Rasim Delic. 158; 391, speaking about continuous offensives; document 378; document 303 which says, and that's 1st January 1995, it says that if this agreement that had just started is observed, use the time to train units and commands and transform the army to continue combat operations. I can give you a lot more of similar examples: D416, 6th of January, 1995, already then it says: "All commands will intensify preparations for carrying out offensive combat and be at readiness to commence with combat offensives." Then D194: "In all defence areas of battalions, prepare positions for firing from machine-guns and anti-aircraft guns." Over the heads of their own population, that's from March 1995. Thus we come to document D163 where Rasim Delic writes to Alija Izetbegovic. I do have to stop and comment on this. It says: "Pursuant to your request and in view of the Presidency session I propose to you the following: The extension of the cease-fire and truce is not acceptable for the following reasons," and then he states the reasons. "Demilitarisation of Sarajevo is also out of the question." And then the most typical thing, the matter that has been discussed at length here, he says to Izetbegovic: "We have to continue saying that we will defend ourselves and will refrain from attacking first (as we have always done)." And document P19, that's Harland's report, says at one point when the offensive had been stopped: "Bosnian media that had already bragged about newly liberated territories now report about the heroic defence of the city by the army." These are the tactics that Izetbegovic talks about. Then you have a series of documents about the offensive in June 1995, it's not even necessary to enumerate them, 392, and so on and so forth. It is noteworthy that in June, not even a month later in fact, on the 8th of July, 1995, there is a new order to launch an offensive, attacks don't stop, then document 151 says Clinton is going for new elections and the US now want a truce. Delic, therefore, issues an order to intensify and activate all combat operations in all theatres of war. And at the end we have another order on the 5th of September when NATO air-strikes had already begun, D424, signed by General Ajdadzic where he says: "We are in constant contact with the UNPROFOR command Sector Sarajevo in order to ensure that all prerequisites are mention for joint action." I can enumerate God knows how many more documents related to these combat operations, because as you remember you allowed me to introduce into evidence a number of documents about these operations. Witness Smith confirmed that the offensive of the BH army that had been long in preparation had started. When you asked, Judge Robinson, whether he remembered if the BH army had opened fire to provoke response from the Serbs, he said he remembered and he said: "We were in the middle of the war." Can we now say it was still a civilian area when all this was going on? This witness also said that the offensive was ongoing on all front lines and Witness Nicolai says the UNPROFOR assumed that fire was intentionally opened in the vicinity of UN positions in the hope that Serbs will respond. This was a regular occurrence, fire was regularly opened from positions held by the BH army in the vicinity of UN positions. Regarding the movements of mortars, he says that it was the objective that CR 1047 -- but soldiers have the right to defend themselves. And whenever they are shot at from certain positions. Proportionality exists if their purpose is to neutralise the enemy's firing point, CR 1054, lines 4 to 7. He says: "In my opinion, the number of shells is not the proper criterion for proportionality. The proper criterion is the accuracy of the target as long as fire is directed at the enemy firing point the response is adequate." Page 1057, lines 17 to 20. He had by that time said a lot about mobile mortars. I have no time to quote. Konings, Knustad, Mohatarem they all speak about these combat operations, but I can mention D219, from which we see that there existed a directive to conduct sabotage operations, the kind of guerilla war that had been tried and tested in the Second World War in that region on the principle destroy and return. There were many sabotage operations of that kind and a lot of evidence about them, and there is a lot of evidence about combat operations in that period when the offensive had started, such as the 16th of June when thousands of shells were fired from one side and a response was called for. Then we have document D118 which says that from the 15th June until the 3rd of July, all weapons we have available are used. And in the final sentence it says: "We evaluated that the number of destroyed combat and non-combat positions is even greater because we fired at them in the circumstances of limited visibility by night when we did not have a proper possibility of observation." In relation to all this evidence I would like to make one point and that's document 519. Why is that document important? P519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't come to the murders yet -- the killings, but P519, that is a report where the following is stated. Captain Hansen informed the liaison officers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that synthetic and UNMO teams were sent to the television buildings. He also asked the liaison officer of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to stop the fire from the Army of BH which was constantly being opened from the PTT building and the surrounding area and from the television building provoking return fire from the Army of Bosnian Serbs in that area. This was requested for the security of the medical team. This was not done, and in the document, as mentioned by Witness Knowles, liaison officer who addressed representatives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, asking them whether there could be a cease-fire for an hour for the safety of the medical and investigation team, but the liaison officer responded, What fire? At that time over 50 heavy artillery shots were registered in front of the PTT building. "Then I asked again whether it was possible for the BH to stop the fire. We could both see the fire in front of the PTT building. The answer again was: 'What fire'? I said this was fire coming from weapons deployed around the PTT building. The BH liaison officer then said probably the Bosnian Serbs would stop firing back if the BH army announced a cease-fire of at least an hour." Why am I reading all this? That was the artillery conflict that went on on the 28th of June when the television building was hit. That was the time when an officer was allegedly jogging in the vicinity while the artillery fighting was going on and saw the air bomb, which two officers who were directly threatened by it said came from the Bosnian side. In this situation I have to say the following with reference to hostages. Who was a hostage and who was whose hostage? Terror and terrorism have been mentioned here. I presented document 415 here. One of the Defence witnesses Sima Tusevljak confirmed here before you, and most of this has already been delivered to The Hague Tribunal and then it was sent back but some of it is still here before you, and that is that during the war so far there is indisputable evidence to show that 2.200 people have been killed, not shot or killed by fire, but slaughtered. And that is another reason why there had to be defence at a time when they were inferior in weapons and manpower. I will slow down now. It's document -- a document of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the security service, it's a confidential document. Let me see. Where should I start? It refers to crimes against humanity and international law perpetrated against civilians, killings in a particularly cruel manner, torture, and the inflicting of enormous suffering, and this even contained elements of genocide. This is their own official report, their own commander is saying that before his eyes they are killing people. These are things that were going on in Sarajevo at the time of the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic, and this completely annihilates this story about who was whose hostage. There were thousands of Serbs there and it would not be easy for anyone to fire on his own people while not responding to fire against them and all this fighting that was going on, just let it go on and simply observe it while people were being killed. And now in order to make the most efficient use of the time, could we have a look at those three clips, so I will show you what Markale was used for and who did that and how it has been misused, how both the living and the dead have been misused, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was never demonstrated whether this hit anyone. All that could be seen was smoke. That was the system on which the entire tactics of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can I ask you, is there an audio part of this also, because we can't hear anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can just hear a bang, but it will take a lot of time. Just a bang and there's smoke. All you can see is smoke. You can't see whether anything has been hit. We should have been able to see the building, to see if anything had been hit there. It's very easy to create a smoke-screen behind which you can see nothing and then show this to the entire world and say that it was done by the Army of Republika Srpska. And all this time the Presidency was a military target. Akashi was in town and they needed a show that day and so the show was put on. Could we see Markale now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was only smoke. Why was there no picture after the smoke had settled? This was simply a show so that Akashi could see what the Serb side was doing, how it was behaving. It was unreasonable to fire on Sarajevo when everybody knew Akashi was there. This was evidently done to show what the people in uniform were like on the other side, in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But, please, can we see Markale now, and don't silence it. It's terrible to see, but that is a truth one has to face. And then I'll try to finish if I can, but it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the film, it's 30 seconds long. You saw only a box and now the terrible scenes you're going to see. You can count as much as you like. I've studied it with experts. There were not more than 25 or 30 people there who were injured or killed. Look at this horror. And now the camera goes back. So all together it's about 30 seconds. Well, you see, that woman wasn't here a little while ago. Now stop. This woman was not here a little while ago. You saw that box there. Underneath this woman there's not a drop of blood. There was some discussion about that. I don't want to waste time on this because the Prosecution case is untenable. Of course this happened, of course there was an explosion there, but I think that in these proceedings we have demonstrated beyond any reasonable doubt that this was a weapon activated under static conditions.
